title: Joshua to Kings: Tribes, Monarchy, Two Kingdoms
bigQuestion: How does the Bible tell the story of Israel's tribes and kings, and what can stones and digs add to that story?

story.title: A Broken Stone at Tel Dan
story.kicker: In the summer of 1993, a surveyor at a dig in northern Israel noticed letters on a stone in a wall.
paragraphs: Tel Dan sits at the far north of Israel, where springs feed the Jordan River. In July 1993, a team led by the archaeologist Avraham Biran was clearing an old city gate there. A member of the team, Gila Cook, saw the afternoon light catch something odd. A flat basalt stone in a wall had lines cut into it. The lines were letters.

The stone was a piece of a stele, a stone slab that a king sets up to brag about a victory. The words were in Aramaic, the language of Israel's neighbors to the north. The king who wrote it was not from Israel. He was telling how he had beaten two enemy kings. Two more pieces turned up the next year.

One line stopped the scholars cold. It named the enemy kingdoms. One was Israel. The other was written as a single word, bytdwd, which most scholars read as "House of David." Until that summer, David's name had never been found on anything outside the Bible. Here it was, cut into stone by an enemy about a hundred and fifty years after the Bible says David lived.

The stone did not prove the Bible's stories about David. It did not say who David was or what he did. It showed something narrower and still important: a kingdom in the south was known to its neighbors, in the 800s BCE, as the house of a founder named David. Some scholars questioned the reading at first. Most now accept it.

This chapter walks through the Bible's own story from Joshua to the fall of Jerusalem. Along the way it stops at three stones and one dig. Each one lets you hold the Bible's account next to a record made by someone else, and ask what fits, what does not, and what neither one says.
story.think: A stone made by Israel's enemy mentions the House of David. What can that stone tell us, and what can it not tell us?

lessons.title: Joshua and the Walls of Jericho
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered Canaan, took Jericho, and divided the land among twelve tribes.
reading: The book of Joshua opens where Deuteronomy ends. Moses has died. The text says God tells Joshua, his helper, to lead the people across the Jordan River into Canaan. In the Jewish Bible, Joshua is the first of the *Former Prophets*, the books that tell Israel's story in the land. Christians count it as the first of the historical books of the Old Testament.

The most famous scene is Jericho (Joshua 6). The story says the people march around the walled city once a day for six days. Priests carry the ark and blow rams' horns. On the seventh day they march seven times, the horns sound, the people shout, and the wall falls flat. Only Rahab, a woman of Jericho who hid Israel's spies, is saved with her family.

The text then describes a hard practice. Jericho and other cities are put under the *ban*, a rule that the city and its people are destroyed as an offering. Readers have wrestled with these chapters for centuries. Jewish and Christian teachers have read them as history, as a warning about idol worship, or as a story shaped to teach later readers. Many scholars note that the book itself says the land was not fully taken (Joshua 13:1).

The second half of Joshua is mostly a map in words. The land is divided by lot among the twelve *tribes*, the large family groups named for Jacob's sons. The book ends at Shechem, where Joshua asks the people to choose whom they will serve, and they renew the covenant.

words.d: in the Jewish Bible, the books Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, which tell Israel's story in the land
the rule in Joshua that a captured city and its people are destroyed as an offering; in Hebrew, herem
the twelve large family groups of Israel, named for the sons of Jacob

look.title: The seventh day at Jericho
look.text: So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city.
look.prompt: List the sounds in this verse in order. Why do you think the story makes noise, not weapons, bring the wall down?

check.q: In the Jewish Bible, the book of Joshua is the first of which group of books?
check.why: Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are the Former Prophets. The Torah ends with Deuteronomy, just before Joshua.

check.q: According to Joshua 6, what happens on the seventh day at Jericho?
choices: The people march seven times, the horns sound, and the wall falls
The city surrenders without a fight
check.why: The text says the people circle the city seven times, the priests blow, the people shout, and the wall falls flat.

check.q: Which statement about the second half of Joshua is correct?
choices: It tells the story of Samson
It divides the land among the twelve tribes
It describes the building of the Temple
check.why: Joshua 13 to 21 divides the land by lot among the tribes. Samson is in Judges; the Temple is in 1 Kings.

lessons.title: What the Ground Says
lessons.mainIdea: Archaeology gives a picture of early Israel that partly matches Joshua and partly does not, and scholars explain the gaps in different ways.
reading: The word *archaeology* means the study of the past through what people left in the ground. That means walls, pots, bones, and writing. It cannot tell us what people believed or who was right. It can tell us when a city was lived in and when it burned. For the time of Joshua and the judges, the *Late Bronze Age* and early Iron Age, the ground gives a mixed answer.

At Jericho, an English dig in the 1930s found fallen walls and said they were Joshua's. Kathleen Kenyon dug again in the 1950s. She dated those walls many centuries earlier. In her view, Jericho was small or empty around 1200 BCE, the time many readers place Joshua. Hazor is different. Its upper city burned around 1230 BCE, which fits Joshua 11:11. Other cities in the list show no sign of a burning at that time.

Two finds matter most. The *Merneptah Stele* is an Egyptian stone from about 1208 BCE. It names "Israel" as a people in Canaan, the oldest mention outside the Bible. And surveys of the hill country show that hundreds of small farming villages appeared after 1200 BCE where few had been before. These villages had simple houses, no temples, and almost no pig bones.

Scholars read the evidence in different ways. Some hold that a quick conquest happened much as Joshua tells it. Others think tribes moved in slowly. Others think many early Israelites were Canaanites who left the cities for the hills. Many today combine these ideas. The Bible's own books leave room for this: Joshua describes a sweeping victory, while Judges 1 lists many cities the tribes did not take.

words.d: the study of the past through things people left behind, such as walls, pottery and inscriptions
the period from about 1550 to 1200 BCE in the eastern Mediterranean, when Egypt ruled Canaan
an Egyptian victory stone from about 1208 BCE that names Israel, the oldest mention outside the Bible

look.title: Events on the ground, around 1200 BCE
rows: Small villages spread in the hills (from about)
Philistine cities grow on the coast (from about)
look.cite: Merneptah Stele, Cairo Museum; Yigael Yadin's Hazor digs (1955-58); Israel Finkelstein, The Archaeology of the Israelite Settlement (1988)
look.prompt: Which of these events fits the book of Joshua best, and which one is hardest to fit? Explain your choice.

check.q: What did Kathleen Kenyon conclude about Jericho's walls?
choices: They fell exactly when Joshua says
They were much older than the time usually given for Joshua
check.why: Kenyon dated Jericho's fallen walls centuries before about 1200 BCE, the time many readers place Joshua.

check.q: Why does the Merneptah Stele matter to historians?
choices: It is the oldest mention of Israel outside the Bible
It describes the fall of Jericho
check.why: The Egyptian stone, from about 1208 BCE, names Israel as a people in Canaan. It says nothing of Jericho or David.

check.q: How does Judges 1 differ from the book of Joshua on the taking of the land?
choices: Judges 1 says the land was taken in one day
Judges 1 lists many cities the tribes did not take
Judges 1 says the tribes never entered Canaan
Judges 1 does not mention the land at all
check.why: Joshua stresses a sweeping victory; Judges 1 names city after city that stayed in Canaanite hands.

lessons.title: Judges in a Crisis
lessons.mainIdea: Judges tells a repeating story of trouble and rescue, with leaders like Deborah, Gideon and Samson, and ends by saying there was no king.
reading: The book of Judges covers the years between Joshua and the first kings. A *judge* here is not a person in a courtroom. A judge is a leader who rises up in a crisis, usually to fight off an enemy. The book has a pattern that repeats like a wheel. The people turn from God, an enemy oppresses them, they cry out, God raises a judge, and the land rests. Then it starts again (Judges 2:11-19). Scholars call this the *cycle* of Judges.

Deborah is a prophet who judges under a palm tree (Judges 4-5). She sends the general Barak against Sisera, whose army has iron chariots. The text says a storm and flood defeat the chariots, and a woman named Jael kills Sisera in her tent. Judges 5 retells the battle as a song. Many scholars think this poem is among the oldest writing in the Bible.

Gideon hides from the Midianites until a messenger calls him a mighty warrior (Judges 6-8). The story says God cuts his army from thousands to three hundred men. They win at night with torches, jars and horns. Samson is the strongest and the strangest judge (Judges 13-16). He is set apart from birth with uncut hair. He fights the Philistines alone, is betrayed by Delilah, and dies pulling down a temple.

The judges get worse as the book goes on. The last chapters tell of civil war. The book's final verse gives its verdict: in those days there was no king, and everyone did what seemed right to them. Readers disagree about that line. Some hear it asking for a king. Others hear it asking for people to keep the covenant. Either way, it sets up the books of Samuel.

words.d: in the book of Judges, a leader who rises in a crisis to rescue the tribes, not a courtroom official
the repeating pattern in Judges: turning away, oppression, crying out, a rescuer, and rest
a people who settled the coast of Canaan around 1175 BCE and fought Israel's tribes and kings

look.title: The last verse of Judges
look.text: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
look.prompt: Is this verse a complaint, a wish for a king, or both? What in the rest of Judges supports your reading?

check.q: In the book of Judges, what is a judge?
choices: A leader who rises in a crisis to rescue the tribes
A scribe who copies the law
check.why: The judges are rescuers in a crisis, such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson. There is no Temple yet and no king.

check.q: Which order matches the cycle in Judges 2?
choices: Turning away, oppression, crying out, a judge, rest
check.why: The pattern begins with turning from God and ends with rest, then repeats.

check.q: Which judge fought the Philistines and was betrayed by Delilah?
check.why: Samson's story is Judges 13 to 16. Gideon fought Midian; Deborah and Barak fought Sisera.

lessons.title: The People Ask for a King
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Samuel the elders ask Samuel for a king, and the text gives both a warning against kings and the start of kingship.
reading: The books of Samuel begin with a woman who cannot have children. Hannah prays at the shrine at Shiloh, and the story says her son Samuel is born and given to serve there (1 Samuel 1-3). Samuel grows up to be a *prophet*, a person who speaks a message from God, and the last of the judges. Meanwhile the Philistines press in from the coast. They even capture the ark, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law (1 Samuel 4).

When Samuel is old, the elders come to him with a demand (1 Samuel 8). They want a king like the other nations. Samuel is not pleased. The text says God tells him the people have rejected God as their king, but to give them what they ask. Samuel warns them what a king will do. He will take their sons for his army, their daughters for his kitchens, and a tenth of their crops. The people insist.

Samuel then finds Saul, a tall young man from the tribe of Benjamin. He pours oil on his head to *anoint* him, that is, to mark him as chosen (1 Samuel 10). The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach, which gives English the word messiah. Saul wins a battle, and the people confirm him as king.

Readers have long noticed that 1 Samuel speaks with two voices. Some chapters treat the king as a gift from God. Others treat kingship as a mistake. Jewish and Christian teachers have read both as true at once: a king can protect the people and also fail them. Many scholars think the two voices come from different sources that an editor joined.

words.d: a person who speaks a message from God to a people or a king
to pour oil on someone's head to mark them as chosen; the Hebrew word gives English messiah
the gold-covered chest that the text says held the tablets of the law; carried into battle in 1 Samuel 4

look.title: The people answer Samuel
look.text: Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, Nay; but we will have a king over us; That we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles.
look.prompt: What three things do the people want a king to do? Which of them do you think worried Samuel most?

check.q: Who was Samuel's mother, according to 1 Samuel 1?
check.why: Hannah prays at Shiloh for a child, and the story says Samuel is born. Deborah is a judge; Rahab is in Joshua.

check.q: What does the word anoint mean?
choices: To write someone's name in a book
To pour oil on someone to mark them as chosen
check.why: Samuel anoints Saul with oil. The Hebrew for anointed one, mashiach, gives English the word messiah.

check.q: Why do many scholars say 1 Samuel speaks with two voices about kings?
choices: Because Samuel and Saul wrote it together
Because it is written in two languages
Because some parts praise kingship and others treat it as a mistake
check.why: Some chapters call the king God's gift; others say asking for a king rejected God. Many scholars think an editor joined different sources.

lessons.title: Saul, David and One Kingdom
lessons.mainIdea: The books of Samuel tell how kingship passed from Saul to David, who made Jerusalem his capital and received a promise about his house.
reading: Saul's reign goes wrong in the text. Twice he disobeys Samuel's instructions, and Samuel tells him God has rejected him (1 Samuel 13 and 15). Samuel then secretly anoints a shepherd boy from Bethlehem named David. David enters Saul's court as a harp player, kills the giant Goliath, and becomes close friends with Saul's son Jonathan. Saul grows jealous and tries to kill him. David flees and lives as an outlaw. Saul dies fighting the Philistines on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31).

Second Samuel tells of David's rule, which the text places around 1000 BCE. He is king of Judah first, then of all the tribes. Historians call this the *united monarchy*. David captures Jerusalem from the Jebusites and makes it his capital (2 Samuel 5). He brings the ark there. He does not build a temple, but in 2 Samuel 7 the prophet Nathan brings him a promise: his house, meaning his family line, will last.

That promise is read in more than one way. Jewish tradition sees in it the hope for a future king from David's line, the *messiah*, who will rule in a time of peace. Christians believe Jesus, whom the Gospels call the son of David, is that king. Historians read 2 Samuel 7 as the founding charter of the Davidic dynasty that ruled Judah for four centuries.

The text does not hide David's faults. He takes Bathsheba, another man's wife, and has her husband Uriah killed in battle (2 Samuel 11). Nathan confronts him with a story about a rich man who steals a poor man's one lamb. David condemns the rich man and then hears the words, You are the man. His later years bring a revolt by his son Absalom. The Bible's picture of its greatest king is a mixed one.

words.d: the historians' name for the time when Saul, David and Solomon ruled all the tribes as one kingdom
an anointed king; in Jewish hope, a future ruler from David's line; Christians believe Jesus is this king
a line of rulers from one family; David's dynasty ruled Judah for about four hundred years

look.title: One promise, three readers
look.text: In 2 Samuel 7 the prophet Nathan tells David that his house and his throne will be made sure forever. A Jewish reader may hear the hope for a messiah from David's line. A Christian reader may hear a promise the Gospels say Jesus fulfilled. A historian may hear the charter of a royal family explaining why it ruled.
look.prompt: Pick two of the three readers. What does each one look for in the passage, and what does each one leave out?

check.q: Where does 2 Samuel 5 say David set up his capital?
check.why: David captured Jerusalem from the Jebusites and made it his capital. Samaria became Israel's capital much later.

check.q: What does Nathan promise David in 2 Samuel 7?
choices: That David will build the Temple
That David's house, his family line, will last
check.why: The promise is about David's house, his dynasty. The text says his son, not David, will build the Temple.

check.q: How does Nathan confront David about Bathsheba and Uriah?
choices: With a story about a rich man who steals a poor man's lamb
With a song from the Psalms
check.why: In 2 Samuel 12 Nathan tells the lamb story, David condemns the rich man, and Nathan says, You are the man.

lessons.title: Solomon and the Temple
lessons.mainIdea: First Kings presents Solomon as a wise builder who raised the Temple in Jerusalem, and also as a king whose burdens and shrines led to trouble.
reading: David's son Solomon takes the throne after a struggle among his brothers. Early in his reign the text says God offers him anything, and Solomon asks for wisdom to judge the people (1 Kings 3). The story of two women who each claim the same baby shows that wisdom in action. Solomon offers to cut the child in half, and the true mother gives it up to save it. Later tradition tied the book of Proverbs to his name.

Solomon's great work is the *Temple* (1 Kings 6-8). The text says it took seven years to build, with cedar from Lebanon sent by King Hiram of Tyre. It had a courtyard, a main hall, and an inner room called the *Holy of Holies*, where the ark was placed. Many scholars date its completion to the 950s BCE. No part of it has been excavated, because the site in Jerusalem is holy to Muslims and Jews today and is not dug.

The text also records the price. Solomon used forced labor gangs and heavy taxes to build his palace, cities and fleet (1 Kings 5 and 9). He married many foreign wives, some for treaties, and 1 Kings 11 says he built shrines for their gods. The book blames these shrines for the troubles that follow. The queen of Sheba's visit (1 Kings 10) shows how far his fame had spread, in the text's telling.

Archaeologists debate how large Solomon's kingdom really was. Some see gates at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer as his work, matching 1 Kings 9:15. Others date those gates a century later. What is not in doubt is the Temple's place in the story. For the rest of Kings, the Temple in Jerusalem is the center that every king is measured against.

words.d: the house of worship Solomon built in Jerusalem, where the text says the ark was kept; the First Temple
the inner room of the Temple, which the text says held the ark; entered only by the high priest
work that people are made to do for a king without choice; 1 Kings says Solomon used it for his buildings

look.title: The Temple's size in 1 Kings 6
look.prompt: Turn the length and width into feet. How does the Temple compare with your school gym? Why might a holy building be smaller than you expected?

check.q: What does 1 Kings 3 say Solomon asked God for?
check.why: Solomon asks for an understanding heart. The story of the two mothers then shows that wisdom at work.

check.q: Why has Solomon's Temple never been excavated?
choices: The site is holy to Muslims and Jews today and is not dug
No one knows which city it was in
It was built of wood and left no trace
Archaeologists have not looked for it
check.why: The Temple Mount in Jerusalem is a sacred site today, so it cannot be excavated.

check.q: What does 1 Kings 11 blame for the troubles after Solomon?
choices: The visit of the queen of Sheba
The shrines he built for his wives' gods
check.why: The text says Solomon's foreign wives led him to build shrines for other gods, and it ties the kingdom's split to that.

lessons.title: The Kingdom Splits
lessons.mainIdea: After Solomon, the text says ten northern tribes broke away as Israel, leaving Judah under David's line, and Kings judges every ruler by one test.
reading: When Solomon died, his son Rehoboam went to Shechem to be made king (1 Kings 12). The northern tribes asked him to lighten the heavy burden of labor and taxes. His older advisers told him to say yes. His young friends told him to answer harshly, and he did. The text says the north replied with a cry: What share do we have in David? To your tents, Israel! Most scholars date this break to about 930 BCE.

From then on there were two kingdoms. The northern one, with ten tribes, kept the name *Israel*. Its first king was Jeroboam, and its capital moved until King Omri built *Samaria* in the 870s BCE. The southern kingdom was *Judah*, with Jerusalem, the Temple, and kings from David's line. To keep his people from going to Jerusalem, the text says Jeroboam set up golden calves at Dan and Bethel. Kings calls this the sin of Jeroboam and never lets it go.

The books of Kings grade every ruler with one sentence: he did what was right, or what was evil, in the eyes of the LORD. The test is loyalty to God and to the Temple in Jerusalem, not wealth or victories. By that test every king of Israel fails, even strong ones like Omri and Ahab. In Judah, a few kings pass. Many scholars think the books were written or finished in Judah, which explains the grading.

The two kingdoms were often at war with each other and sometimes allied. Israel was larger and richer, with better farmland and trade routes. Judah was smaller and poorer but had the Temple and the Davidic line. Prophets such as Elijah and Elisha worked in Israel; Isaiah and Micah worked in Judah. The story of both kingdoms runs side by side through 1 and 2 Kings.

words.d: after about 930 BCE, the northern kingdom of ten tribes, with its capital at Samaria
the southern kingdom, ruled from Jerusalem by kings of David's line
the capital city that King Omri built for the northern kingdom in the 870s BCE

look.title: The north walks out
look.text: So when all Israel saw that the king hearkened not unto them, the people answered the king, saying, What portion have we in David? neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David. So Israel departed unto their tents.
look.prompt: Rehoboam is never named in this verse. Who is named instead, and what does that tell you about what the north was rejecting?

check.q: What did the northern tribes ask Rehoboam to do at Shechem?
choices: Lighten the burden of labor and taxes
check.why: They asked for a lighter yoke. His harsh answer led to the break, which most scholars date to about 930 BCE.

check.q: Which was true of the southern kingdom of Judah?
choices: Its kings came from David's line and it kept Jerusalem
check.why: Judah kept Jerusalem, the Temple and the Davidic dynasty. Samaria, ten tribes and Jeroboam belong to the north.

check.q: By what test do the books of Kings grade each ruler?
choices: Loyalty to God and the Temple in Jerusalem
The number of cities he built
check.why: Each king did right or evil in the eyes of the LORD. Wealth and victories do not count in this grading.

lessons.title: Assyria Takes Samaria
lessons.mainIdea: The Assyrian empire pressed Israel for tribute for a century and then, in 722 BCE, captured Samaria and deported its people.
reading: *Assyria* was an empire in the north of what is now Iraq, with great cities at Ashur and Nineveh. From the 800s BCE its armies marched west almost every year. Smaller kingdoms could pay *tribute*, that is, yearly gifts of silver, gold and goods, or be crushed. A carved black stone in the British Museum, the Black Obelisk of about 825 BCE, shows Israel's King Jehu bowing before the Assyrian king. It is the only known picture of an Israelite king.

Under Tiglath-pileser III, from 745 BCE, Assyria began taking land, not just tribute. Second Kings 15 says he carried off people from Israel's north. When Israel's last king, Hoshea, stopped paying and looked to Egypt for help, Assyria besieged Samaria. The city fell in 722 BCE after about three years (2 Kings 17:5-6). Assyrian records agree, and King Sargon II claims the victory and says he carried off about 27,000 people.

The practice of *deportation* was Assyria's policy. Leaders, craftsmen and soldiers were moved to distant parts of the empire, and other peoples were settled in their place. Second Kings 17 says foreigners were brought to Samaria's towns. Israel's northern tribes never returned as a group. Later legends spoke of ten lost tribes. Jewish tradition connects the mixed population of the region with the Samaritans of later centuries.

The text explains the fall in its own way. Second Kings 17 gives a long sermon: Israel fell because it worshiped other gods and ignored the prophets. A historian would add Assyria's strength, Hoshea's gamble on Egypt, and Samaria's position on the road to Egypt. Both explanations are in the chapter, one stated and one visible in the events.

words.d: an empire in northern Mesopotamia, with capitals at Ashur and Nineveh, that conquered Israel in 722 BCE
yearly payments in silver, gold and goods that a small kingdom made to an empire to avoid attack
forcing a conquered people to move to another part of an empire; Assyria's policy after a revolt

look.title: The fall of Samaria in Kings
look.text: In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
look.prompt: The verse names the places the people were sent. Why might the writer list them instead of just saying far away?

check.q: What does the Black Obelisk show?
choices: Israel's King Jehu bowing before the Assyrian king
check.why: The Black Obelisk of about 825 BCE, in the British Museum, is the only known picture of an Israelite king, Jehu.

check.q: In what year did Samaria fall to Assyria?
check.why: Samaria fell in 722 BCE. The kingdom split about 930 BCE, and Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BCE.

check.q: What was Assyria's policy of deportation?
choices: Making conquered people pay in silver
Moving conquered people to distant parts of the empire and settling others in their place
check.why: Deportation moved leaders and craftsmen away and brought in outsiders. Tribute, not deportation, was payment in silver.

lessons.title: Hezekiah, Josiah and the Fall of Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: Judah survived Assyria under Hezekiah, reformed under Josiah, and then fell to Babylon, which burned the Temple in 586 BCE.
reading: Judah watched Samaria fall and lasted another 136 years. King Hezekiah, who ruled from about 715 BCE, cut a tunnel through rock to bring water inside Jerusalem's walls. Visitors can still walk it. Then he rebelled against Assyria. In 701 BCE King Sennacherib invaded, destroyed the city of Lachish, and camped around Jerusalem. Second Kings 18-19 says the prophet Isaiah told Hezekiah the city would stand, and that an angel struck the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib's own record says Hezekiah paid heavy tribute. Both agree Jerusalem was not taken.

Two generations later King Josiah, who ruled from about 640 BCE, led a *reform*. Second Kings 22 says workers repairing the Temple found a book of the law, and Josiah tore his clothes when it was read. He closed shrines outside Jerusalem and kept a great Passover. Many scholars think the book was an early form of Deuteronomy. Josiah died in battle at Megiddo in 609 BCE, and his reform faded.

By then Assyria was collapsing. Its capital Nineveh fell to *Babylon* and its allies in 612 BCE. Babylon's King Nebuchadnezzar became the new master of the region. Judah's kings switched sides between Babylon and Egypt. In 597 BCE Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and carried off King Jehoiachin with thousands of others. Clay tablets found in Babylon list food rations for Jehoiachin, king of Judah, by name.

The last king, Zedekiah, rebelled again. Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem for about a year and a half. In 586 BCE the walls were breached, the Temple was burned, and more people were deported (2 Kings 25). Some scholars date the fall to 587 BCE. The book of Kings ends in Babylon, with Jehoiachin released from prison and eating at the king's table. It is a quiet ending that leaves a door open.

words.d: a change that a ruler makes to fix how things are done; Josiah's reform closed shrines outside Jerusalem
the empire in southern Mesopotamia that replaced Assyria and took Jerusalem in 597 and 586 BCE
surrounding a city with an army so no one can get in or out, until it surrenders or falls

look.title: The Temple burns
look.text: And he burnt the house of the LORD, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire.
look.prompt: The verse is one plain sentence with no feeling words. Why might the writer report the worst day in the book this way?

check.q: What did Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BCE end with, according to both the Bible and the Assyrian record?
check.why: Kings says an angel struck the camp; Sennacherib says Hezekiah paid tribute. Both agree the city was not taken.

check.q: What do many scholars think the book found in the Temple under Josiah was?
check.why: Josiah's reform matches Deuteronomy's demands, so many scholars link the book of 2 Kings 22 to it.

check.q: Which event happened in 586 BCE?
choices: Babylon burned Jerusalem and the Temple
check.why: Babylon took Jerusalem and burned the Temple in 586 BCE. Samaria fell in 722, Nineveh in 612, and the split was about 930.

lessons.title: The House of David Stone
lessons.mainIdea: The Tel Dan stele, found in 1993, is an enemy king's record that names the House of David, the first mention of David outside the Bible.
reading: A *stele* is a standing stone with words or pictures cut into it. Ancient kings set them up to record victories and to warn enemies. Most steles from Israel's neighbors have been lost or broken. That makes the three pieces found at Tel Dan in 1993 and 1994 unusual. They had been reused as building stones in a wall, which is why they survived.

The *inscription* is in Aramaic. The king who set it up was from Aram, the kingdom around Damascus. Most scholars think he was Hazael, who fought Israel in the 840s BCE and appears in 2 Kings 8-13. He boasts that he killed a king of Israel and a king of the House of David. The names are damaged, but the surviving letters fit Jehoram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah. Second Kings 9 says those two kings died together, though it credits Jehu, not Hazael.

The stone matters for two reasons. First, it shows that in the 800s BCE Judah was known by its neighbors as the dynasty of David. Second, it shows how two records can tell one event differently. Hazael claims the kills. Kings gives them to Jehu, a general who may have acted with Aram's support. A historian holds both accounts and asks what each writer wanted readers to believe.

A few scholars argued that bytdwd could mean something other than House of David, such as a place name. Most scholars reject those readings. The stele is now in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem. It cannot tell us whether David fought Goliath or wrote psalms. It tells us that a kingdom carried his name.

choices: A clay tablet used for school lessons
A coin with a king's face
A standing stone with words or pictures cut into it
check.why: Kings set up steles to record victories. The Tel Dan and Mesha stones are both steles.

check.q: Why is the Tel Dan stele important to historians?

It proves David wrote the Psalms
It was written by King David
It describes the building of the Temple

check.why: The stele was set up by a king of Aram, and Aramaic was that kingdom's language.

lessons.title: King Mesha's Side of the Story
lessons.mainIdea: The Mesha stele lets us read a war between Israel and Moab from the Moabite king's point of view and set it beside 2 Kings 3.
reading: *Moab* was a kingdom east of the Dead Sea, in what is now Jordan. Second Kings 3 says Moab's King Mesha had paid Israel tribute in lambs and wool, and that he rebelled when King Ahab died. In 1868 a missionary named Frederick Klein was shown a black stone near the town of Dhiban. It was covered in writing. Before it could be bought, local people broke it in pieces, but a paper copy of the writing had been made. The stone was pieced together and is now in the Louvre in Paris.

The stone is Mesha's own account, in the Moabite language, which is very close to Hebrew. Mesha says that Omri, king of Israel, had oppressed Moab for many years because *Chemosh*, the god of Moab, was angry with his land. Then Chemosh gave Mesha victory, and he took back towns and built cities. The stele, from about 840 BCE, names Israel, Omri, and the God of Israel by the letters YHWH. It is one of the oldest inscriptions to do so.

Read the two accounts together. Kings says Israel, Judah and Edom invaded Moab and won until Mesha made a terrible sacrifice on the wall. Then the armies pulled back (2 Kings 3:27). Mesha says nothing about losing. He tells only of victories. Both writers give their god credit for what happened. Both leave out what would make their own side look bad.

This is how ancient royal writing worked. A king's stone is not a newspaper. It is a claim. The books of Kings are not a newspaper either. They are a story told to teach. Historians hold the two beside each other and look for what neither writer had reason to invent, like the names of kings and cities.

words.d: a kingdom east of the Dead Sea, in today's Jordan, that fought with Israel in the 800s BCE
the god of Moab, whom the Mesha stele credits with Moab's victory over Israel

look.title: Two kings, one war
look.text: Mesha's stone: Omri of Israel oppressed Moab for many days because Chemosh was angry. Chemosh gave Moab victory, and Mesha took back the towns. Kings 3: after Ahab died, Mesha rebelled. Israel and its allies beat Moab in the field, until Mesha sacrificed his own son on the wall and the armies withdrew.

check.q: Whom does the Mesha stele credit with Moab's victory?
check.why: Mesha says Chemosh was angry, then gave Moab victory. Omri is the Israelite king he says oppressed Moab.

check.q: What does 2 Kings 3 say happened at the end of the war with Moab?
choices: Mesha made a sacrifice on the wall and the armies withdrew
check.why: 2 Kings 3:27 reports Mesha's sacrifice of his son and the withdrawal. Mesha's stone does not mention this.

check.q: Where is the Mesha stele kept today?
check.why: The Mesha stele is in the Louvre. The Tel Dan stele is in Jerusalem and the Black Obelisk is in London.

lessons.title: Sennacherib's Prism in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Sennacherib's clay prism gives Assyria's account of the 701 BCE attack on Judah, and a copy of it sits in a museum in Chicago.
reading: Assyrian kings kept *annals*, year-by-year records of their campaigns, written on clay. Sennacherib's annals were pressed into a six-sided clay *prism* in *cuneiform*, the wedge-shaped script of Mesopotamia. Three nearly complete copies survive. One, the Taylor Prism, is in the British Museum. One is in the Israel Museum. The third is at the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures at the University of Chicago, which bought it in 1919. Students in Illinois can stand in front of it.

The prism describes the campaign of 701 BCE. Sennacherib says he took 46 walled cities of Judah and many villages, and drove out more than 200,000 people and their animals. Then comes the famous line about Hezekiah: Sennacherib says he shut him up in Jerusalem, his royal city, like a bird in a cage. He lists Hezekiah's tribute, including 30 talents of gold and 800 talents of silver.

Now open 2 Kings 18-19. It agrees that Sennacherib took Judah's fortified cities and that Hezekiah paid 30 talents of gold, though it says 300 talents of silver. It agrees that Jerusalem did not fall. It disagrees about why. Kings says an angel struck the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib went home. The prism never claims to have entered Jerusalem, which is unusual for an Assyrian king. Historians have suggested disease, trouble at home, or a deal.

Sennacherib also had the siege of Lachish carved on his palace walls at Nineveh. Those carvings, now in the British Museum, show battering rams, captives, and the king on his throne. The Bible mentions Lachish only in passing. An Assyrian king put it at the center of his palace. Each side told the part of the story that made it look strong.

As a king who surrendered his city

review.q: Which group of books does Jewish tradition call the Former Prophets?
review.why: The Former Prophets tell Israel's story in the land. Genesis to Deuteronomy is the Torah.

review.q: What is the oldest mention of Israel outside the Bible?
choices: The Merneptah Stele of about 1208 BCE
review.why: The Egyptian Merneptah Stele names Israel as a people in Canaan. The other three stones are from the 800s and 700s BCE.

review.q: Which sentence best describes the pattern in the book of Judges?
choices: Prophets write letters to the Temple
The people turn away, are oppressed, cry out, and a judge rescues them
Priests divide the land by lot
review.why: Judges 2 sets out the cycle. Dividing the land is in Joshua; kings come in Samuel and Kings.

review.q: Which king does the text say built the First Temple in Jerusalem?
review.why: 1 Kings 6 says Solomon built the Temple. David wanted to but the text says his son would do it.

review.q: About when did the kingdom split into Israel and Judah?
review.why: The split under Rehoboam is dated about 930 BCE. 722 is the fall of Samaria and 586 the fall of Jerusalem.

review.q: Which empire destroyed Samaria, and which destroyed Jerusalem?
choices: Assyria took Samaria; Babylon took Jerusalem
Babylon took Samaria; Assyria took Jerusalem
review.why: Assyria captured Samaria in 722 BCE. Babylon burned Jerusalem in 586 BCE. Persia came later and let exiles return.

review.q: What do the Tel Dan and Mesha steles have in common?
choices: Both were written by kings of Israel
Both are in the British Museum
Both are records by Israel's neighbors that mention Israel
Both describe the fall of Jerusalem
review.why: An Aramean king made the Tel Dan stele and a Moabite king made the Mesha stele. Each tells of war with Israel.

review.q: A student says: The Bible and Sennacherib's prism agree on everything about 701 BCE. What is the best correction?
choices: The Bible does not mention Sennacherib
They agree Jerusalem was not taken but differ on why and on the amount of silver
review.why: Both say Sennacherib took Judah's cities but not Jerusalem. Kings credits an angel; the prism lists tribute, with 800 talents of silver to Kings' 300.
